column8:
In my contracts I've used hourly rates as justification & reference for flat rates. If I think a project might take 20 hours, I'll put $1200 down as the total. Of course, I don't think I've ever actually finished a project in that time (client needs edits, data takes longer than expected to process...) so if it were truly "hourly" I'd definitely be charging more. Try to account for that in the contract via solid scoping.

That said, it really depends on the client! For friends or passion projects, $15/hr is fine by me. Larger organizations with actual budgets are gonna see a higher rate than small non-profits.

Gouge, gouge, gouge! Good-looking cartography is still a pain in the ass and relatively few people do it, so you can and should charge a shitload for your time. Hourly has perverse incentives, get a flat rate contract with a specific number of revisions.

column8:
I've only used one online visualization graphic design site/service (I'll omit their name) to, in the past, accept freelance work. Generally the project requests ranged from $800 - $1,200 per. The service adeptly and promptly handled  brokering, invitation, communications, and payment. Project management was well defined, but the customers were, almost without exception, unclear in what turned out to be their actual goals, which tended to be quite different than those described in the project invitation. I suspect it is a combination of (at least) two factors...
1. Maps are more of an analytical domain than the typical graphic design project involves. As such it can be really difficult to safely arrive at a mutual understanding without essentially making, then iterating, maps to show as a "mockup" while simple "changes" are full re-builds with variable effort. External examples were helpful, but I found the customers' mind's eyes were frequently quite different from cited examples in critical (and time consuming) ways.
2. I suspect the sort of organization that uses a brokering service like this is a risky (to a contractor) combination of A) too underfunded to fully engage with a firm or specialized employee, but B) ambitious enough to seek an outside service. This can create an environment of (understandably) entitled excellence but engaging in projects that are more specialized than they suspect.
